html:
The stone spheres of Costa Rica are hundreds of near-perfect stone balls made by the people of the Diquís delta in the south of the country, mostly between about 500 and 1500 CE. The largest are over two metres across.

They were shaped from granite-like rock by pecking and grinding, and set in lines and groups in front of chiefs' houses and plazas. Their meaning is unknown; they may have marked rank or the power of a chiefdom. Most were moved when banana companies cleared the delta in the 1930s, and many now sit in gardens and public buildings.

In 2014 four settlements with spheres became a World Heritage Site. With Guayabo, they show the chiefdoms of Costa Rica that lay between the Maya world and the cultures of Colombia.
